passage:
Sachin wanted to learn chess. He picked Tuesday and Saturday evenings, one hour each, right after homework, and told his family at dinner: "That's my chess time." His sister stopped asking him to play cards on those days.

Jasleen started drawing with only ten minutes a day. She thought a tiny habit that carried on beat a big plan that fizzled after three days. By the end of a month, her sketchbook was half full.

Lokesh spent a whole week on a rainbow timetable for painting and a trip to buy brushes, paints and three sizes of paper. He pinned the timetable above his bed and admired it. At the end of the week, the paper was still white, and he had not painted a stroke.

Mira painted every afternoon, until exams came near. She cut it to Sunday mornings only, and wrote on her calendar, "Full time again after the last paper." She kept her brush wet on Sundays, and the painting stayed alive.

qa.q: Which evenings did Sachin set aside for chess?
qa.a: He set aside Tuesday and Saturday evenings.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh's week produce no painting while Jasleen's and Mira's routines continued?
qa.a: Lokesh spent the week planning and buying supplies without painting, while Jasleen kept a tiny daily habit and Mira cut down to Sundays during exams instead of quitting.

qa.q: What might Lokesh be feeling at the end of the week?
qa.a: A bit embarrassed and disappointed, since the paper was still white despite all the preparation.
Lokesh could paint for ten minutes today with what he already has, and adjust the timetable later.

grounding: Four approaches to a hobby routine: a fixed slot, starting small, planning without starting, and reducing time during exams.
